title: The Perfect Phone Up Opening
description: Master the first 15 seconds of every inbound call: warm greeting, name exchange, and creating instant trust with a customer who's never spoken to you before.

modules.title: The Greeting Formula
modules.objective: Answer every call with a greeting that wins the customer in 5 words
modules.lesson:
The Greeting Formula

When a customer calls a dealership, the first voice they hear sets the tone for everything. A flat, robotic greeting signals that this call will be like every other dealership call they've dreaded. A warm, confident greeting does the opposite — it tells them this experience is going to be different.

The Formula

Your name → Dealership → Warm opener

Example: "Good afternoon, this is Marcus at Riverside Toyota — thanks for calling in, how can I help you today?"

What to Avoid

  • "Yeah?" or "Hello?" — sounds like you don't work there
  • "Riverside Toyota sales department, please hold" — puts them on hold before they speak
  • A monotone, rushed delivery — customers can hear a smile through the phone
  • Mumbling your name — they need to know who they're talking to

The Smile Rule

Studies show that smiling while speaking changes the resonance of your voice in ways listeners detect subconsciously. Before every call, plant your feet, sit up straight, and smile — then answer.

Practice Goal

Ashley is calling in about a vehicle she saw online. Your job starts the moment you say hello. Nail the greeting and make her feel like she called the right place.

modules.title: Getting Their Name First
modules.objective: Capture the caller's name naturally within the first 20 seconds
modules.lesson:
Getting Their Name First

The single most important thing you can do in the first 30 seconds of a call is learn the customer's name. Not because it's polite — although it is — but because it fundamentally changes the entire conversation. A person who has given you their name is 3x more likely to give you their phone number. They've started saying yes.

The Natural Ask

Don't wait. Ask early, before the customer has a chance to fire questions at you.
"Before I look that up, who am I speaking with?"
"Happy to help! I'm Marcus — and your name?"

The Reciprocity Principle

Always give your name first. When you introduce yourself, the customer feels a social obligation to reciprocate. It's not manipulation — it's basic human connection. Use it.

Using Their Name

Once you have it: use it. Not every sentence — that's annoying — but 2-3 times naturally throughout the call. It signals attentiveness and builds rapport faster than any other technique.

Practice Goal

Tyler is a first-time buyer who's a little hesitant. Get his name in the first exchange and use it at least twice more in the call. Your discovery score depends on the connection you build.

modules.title: Setting the Tone
modules.objective: Immediately differentiate yourself from every other dealership they've called
modules.lesson:
Setting the Tone

Most salespeople answer calls in survival mode — just trying not to say something wrong. The reps who win set the tone proactively. They signal, from the very first sentence, that this call is going to be different.

The Differentiation Signal

Customers call multiple dealerships. They're used to being transferred, put on hold, or immediately pitched. Break the pattern:
"I'm not going to throw a bunch of numbers at you — let me just ask a couple quick questions so I can actually point you in the right direction."

The Honesty Disarm

One of the most powerful openers is radical transparency:
"Fair warning — I'm going to ask you a few questions before I answer yours, because otherwise I'd just be guessing. Cool?"
This reframes you as a consultant, not a salesperson.

Pace and Energy

Match the customer's energy within the first 30 seconds. If they're excited, match it. If they're measured and businesslike, match that. Mismatched energy is one of the fastest rapport-killers on the phone.

Practice Goal

James is a retired teacher — patient and thoughtful. Your tone should be warm and unhurried. Don't rush him. Earn his trust before you ask anything.

modules.title: The First 15 Seconds
modules.objective: Execute a flawless opening that sets up everything that follows
modules.lesson:
The First 15 Seconds

Research on phone conversations shows that lasting impressions are formed in the first 15 seconds. Not the first minute — 15 seconds. Everything you do in that window shapes whether the customer treats you as a trusted advisor or just another salesperson trying to get their money.

The 15-Second Checklist

  1. Warm greeting — smile in your voice, dealership name, your name
  2. Affirm their call — "Thanks for calling" or "Glad you reached out"
  3. Get their name — before diving into their question
  4. Confirm the inquiry — "What can I help you with today?" or "What brought you in to call us?"

What Not to Do in the First 15 Seconds

  • Transfer them
  • Put them on hold
  • Ask for their phone number before building any rapport
  • Launch into a pitch about inventory or specials

Practice Goal

Margaret has never bought a car alone before. She needs to feel safe and unhurried from your very first word. Your opening 15 seconds need to earn that trust.

modules.title: Opening Under Pressure
modules.objective: Maintain a perfect opening even when the customer comes in hot
modules.lesson:
Opening Under Pressure

Not every call starts on friendly terms. Some customers call already frustrated — maybe they submitted a lead form hours ago and nobody called back. Maybe they got a bad quote from a competitor. Maybe they're just having a bad day. Your opening needs to work even when you're walking into a wall of hostility.

The Pressure Opening

When a customer is already upset:
1. Don't match their energy (don't be aggressive or defensive)
2. Don't over-apologize (it signals weakness)
3. Acknowledge and redirect: "I hear you — let me focus on making this right for you right now."

The One-Sentence Reset

If a customer is already on the attack, one sentence can reset the energy:
"I completely understand — honestly, let's skip the back-and-forth and figure out what actually works for you."

Staying Calm

Your physiological calm is contagious. When you stay steady and warm, most customers de-escalate within 60 seconds. You can't control how they start the call — only how you respond to it.

Practice Goal

Nina is analytical and direct — she'll ask pointed questions immediately and expect direct answers. Your job is to open with clarity and confidence, not scramble to catch up.
